meta.titre: Animal Tissues: Matching Structure to Function
meta.sous_theme: Epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue

sections.contenu_markdown: At Mile 17 market in Buea, a butcher cuts a goat carcass into portions. In a few strokes he separates red lean meat, shiny white strips that join the meat to the bone, creamy sheets of fat and a hard, white bone. These are samples of the four tissue families found in every animal body: epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue. The GCE A Level paper regularly asks you to identify a tissue from a short description of its cells, its matrix and its position, or to explain how a structure suits a function. Learning the tissues as a set of contrasting features is the quickest way to score these marks.

items: A tissue is a group of similar cells, together with the products they secrete, that work together to perform a particular function.
During early embryonic development three germ layers form: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, and every tissue of the adult body develops from one or more of them.
Collagen is a strong, fibrous, non-elastic protein that resists stretching, while elastin is a fibrous protein that stretches and recoils.
The extracellular matrix is the material secreted by cells and lying outside them; it is made of fibres embedded in a ground substance.

sections.titre: The four basic animal tissues and how to tell them apart
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Epithelial tissue** forms continuous sheets that cover body surfaces and line cavities, tubes and ducts. Its cells are packed tightly together with very little extracellular matrix, and they rest on a **basement membrane** made of collagen and glycoproteins. Epithelia contain no blood vessels (they are avascular) and receive oxygen and nutrients by diffusion from the connective tissue beneath. Their cells are replaced quickly by mitosis. The functions are protection, secretion, absorption and filtration. Epithelial tissues arise from **all three germ layers**: the epidermis from ectoderm, the lining of the gut and airways from endoderm, and the lining of blood vessels and kidney tubules from mesoderm.

**Connective tissue** has few cells scattered in a large amount of extracellular matrix that the cells secrete. It binds, supports and connects other tissues and arises from mesoderm. Examples are areolar tissue, adipose tissue, dense fibrous tissue (tendons and ligaments), cartilage, bone and blood.

**Muscle tissue** is made of elongated cells (fibres) rich in the contractile proteins actin and myosin. Contraction shortens the fibres and produces movement.

**Nervous tissue** consists of **neurones**, which generate and conduct impulses, and **neuroglia**, which support and protect the neurones.

A reliable method for any identification question is to ask four things in order: (1) Are the cells packed in a sheet on a basement membrane, or separated by matrix? (2) If there is matrix, is it fluid, flexible and solid, or hard and mineralised? (3) Do the cells contain visible striations or contract? (4) Is there a cell body with long processes?

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use when a question describes a lining or covering tissue and asks for its name, site or function.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Epithelium | Cell shape and layers | Typical site | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simple squamous | One layer of thin flat cells | Alveoli of the lungs, walls of capillaries | Short diffusion path for gases and solutes |
| Simple cuboidal | One layer of cube-shaped cells | Kidney tubules, salivary glands | Secretion and absorption |
| Simple columnar | One layer of tall cells, often with microvilli and goblet cells | Lining of the small intestine | Absorption and secretion of mucus |
| Ciliated columnar | Tall cells bearing cilia, with goblet cells | Trachea, bronchi, oviduct | Moves mucus or an egg along the tube |
| Stratified squamous | Many layers, surface cells flat | Epidermis of the skin, lining of the mouth | Protection against abrasion and water loss |

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use when a question asks you to distinguish the two skeletal connective tissues or to state where each cell type comes from.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Feature | Hyaline cartilage | Bone |
|---|---|---|
| Cells | Chondrocytes in lacunae; derived from chondroblasts | Osteocytes in lacunae joined by canaliculi; derived from osteoblasts |
| Matrix | Collagen fibres in a firm, flexible gel of chondroitin sulphate | Collagen fibres hardened with calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) |
| Blood supply | None (avascular); nutrients diffuse from the perichondrium | Rich supply through central canals and the marrow |
| Sites | Ends of long bones, trachea rings, nose, embryonic skeleton | Skeleton: compact bone in the shaft, spongy bone with trabeculae in the epiphyses |
| Repair | Slow | Fairly rapid |

In compact bone the osteocytes lie in concentric rings around a central Haversian canal that carries blood vessels and nerves; the canaliculi are tiny channels that let neighbouring osteocytes exchange materials. Osteocytes are mature osteoblasts that have become trapped in the matrix they secreted. Tendons are dense fibrous connective tissue joining muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use when a question asks you to compare muscle types or to link a structure to a site in the body.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Feature | Skeletal | Smooth | Cardiac |
|---|---|---|---|
| Striations | Present | Absent | Present |
| Nuclei | Many per fibre, at the edge | One per cell, central | One or two per cell, central |
| Cell shape | Long, unbranched cylinders | Spindle-shaped | Short, branched, joined by intercalated discs |
| Control | Voluntary | Involuntary | Involuntary (myogenic) |
| Fatigue | Fatigues quickly | Fatigues slowly | Does not fatigue |
| Site | Attached to bones by tendons | Walls of gut, blood vessels, bladder | Wall of the heart |

sections.enonce_markdown:
A student examines three prepared slides under a light microscope and records the following observations.

- **Slide P:** a single layer of very thin, flattened cells with flat nuclei, resting on a thin basement membrane. The material comes from the wall of an air sac of the lung.
- **Slide Q:** long, cylindrical, unbranched cells with several nuclei at the edge of each cell and regular cross-striations. The material is attached to a bone by a white cord.
- **Slide R:** round cells lying singly or in pairs inside small spaces in a firm, smooth matrix. There are no blood vessels and no fine channels joining the spaces. The material comes from the ring that keeps the trachea open.

(a) Identify each tissue and give the features that support your decision. (b) On slide Q the width of one fibre measures 15 mm on the photomicrograph, which has a magnification of ×300. Calculate the actual width of the fibre in micrometres.

etapes.action: Look at the arrangement of the cells and their position in the organ for Slide P.
etapes.justification: A single sheet of cells on a basement membrane with no matrix is the signature of an epithelium; the shape decides which one.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Cells are thin and flat, so the tissue is **simple squamous epithelium**. The thin cells give a short diffusion distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide between air and blood.

etapes.action: Analyse the cell structure and the attachment for Slide Q.
etapes.justification: Striations, many nuclei per fibre and attachment to bone by a tendon are the features of voluntary muscle.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The tissue is **skeletal (striated) muscle**: long multinucleate fibres whose regular actin and myosin filaments give the striations.

etapes.action: Analyse the matrix and the cell positions for Slide R.
etapes.justification: Cells in lacunae within a firm flexible matrix with no blood vessels and no canaliculi cannot be bone, which has canaliculi and a blood supply.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The tissue is **hyaline cartilage**; the chondrocytes lie in lacunae and the rings keep the trachea open while allowing it to bend.

etapes.action: Convert the image measurement to an actual size using the magnification formula.
etapes.justification: Actual size = image size divided by magnification, and the image size must be converted into micrometres (1 mm = 1000 µm).
The magnification states how many times larger the image is than the real object.

sections.conclusion_markdown: P is simple squamous epithelium, Q is skeletal muscle and R is hyaline cartilage. The fibre in slide Q is 50 µm wide. In every identification question, quote the observable feature first and then name the tissue.

items.erreur_markdown: "Cartilage has a good blood supply, so it heals as fast as bone."
items.pourquoi_faux: Cartilage is avascular. Its chondrocytes receive nutrients only by diffusion through the matrix from the surrounding perichondrium, which makes repair slow.
items.correction_markdown: Cartilage has **no blood vessels** and heals slowly; bone has a rich blood supply and repairs relatively quickly.

items.erreur_markdown: "Cardiac muscle is smooth muscle because it works involuntarily."
items.pourquoi_faux: The type of muscle is decided by its microscopic structure, not by whether it is under conscious control. Cardiac fibres show striations like skeletal muscle.
items.correction_markdown: Cardiac muscle is **striated and involuntary**, with branched fibres joined by intercalated discs. Smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary.

items.erreur_markdown: "Epithelial tissue has a rich blood supply and a lot of matrix."
items.pourquoi_faux: Epithelial cells are packed tightly together with very little matrix and no blood vessels. It is connective tissue that has abundant matrix.
items.correction_markdown: Epithelium is **avascular**, sits on a basement membrane and gets its supplies by diffusion from the underlying connective tissue.

items.erreur_markdown: "Tendons join bone to bone and ligaments join muscle to bone."
items.pourquoi_faux: The two are swapped. Both are dense fibrous connective tissue, but they connect different structures.
items.correction_markdown: **Tendons** join muscle to bone; **ligaments** join bone to bone at joints.

items.erreur_markdown: "Skeletal muscle fibres have a single nucleus in the centre."
items.pourquoi_faux: Skeletal muscle fibres form by the fusion of many cells, so each fibre has many nuclei lying just beneath the cell surface. A single central nucleus is a feature of smooth muscle cells.
items.correction_markdown: Skeletal muscle fibres are **multinucleate** with nuclei at the periphery.

items.enonce_markdown:
Name the tissue described in each case.

(a) Tall cells with hair-like projections and mucus-secreting goblet cells lining the windpipe.

(b) A cord of parallel collagen fibres that joins the calf muscle to the heel bone.

(c) Spindle-shaped, non-striated cells with one central nucleus in the wall of the small intestine.

(d) Large cells that store triglyceride in a droplet under the skin and insulate the body.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Ciliated columnar epithelium**: the cilia move mucus and trapped dust upwards.

(b) **Tendon (dense fibrous connective tissue)**: it joins muscle to bone.

(c) **Smooth muscle**: spindle-shaped, uninucleate and without striations.

(d) **Adipose tissue**: a connective tissue specialised for fat storage and insulation.

items.enonce_markdown:
Explain how each structure is adapted to its function.

(a) The simple squamous epithelium that forms the wall of a capillary.

(b) The branched fibres and intercalated discs of cardiac muscle.

(c) The concentric Haversian systems of compact bone in the shaft of the femur.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The cells are only one cell thick and very flat, so the diffusion distance between blood and tissue fluid is short; the smooth lining also reduces friction with the flowing blood.

(b) Branching links the fibres into a network so that the wave of contraction spreads quickly through the walls of the chamber; the intercalated discs contain gap junctions that let the electrical signal pass from cell to cell, so the cells contract in a coordinated way; the muscle is myogenic and does not fatigue.

(c) Each Haversian system has layers (lamellae) of hard, collagen-reinforced matrix in concentric rings, which gives the shaft strength against bending and compression; the central canal carries blood vessels and nerves, and canaliculi link the osteocytes to this supply, so that the living cells deep in the hard matrix still receive nutrients and oxygen.

items.enonce_markdown:
A drawing of one cardiac muscle cell made from a photomicrograph is 54 mm long. The actual cell is 90 µm long.

(a) Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

(b) The nucleus in the drawing is 9 mm wide. Calculate its actual width.

(c) State two structural differences between cardiac muscle and skeletal muscle that the student could observe on the slide.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Magnification = image length ÷ actual length. Convert 54 mm to 54 000 µm. Magnification = 54 000 ÷ 90 = **×600**.

(b) Convert 9 mm to 9 000 µm. Actual width = 9 000 ÷ 600 = **15 µm**.

(c) Cardiac fibres are short and branched and are joined end to end by intercalated discs, whereas skeletal fibres are long, unbranched cylinders; each cardiac cell has one or two central nuclei, whereas a skeletal fibre has many nuclei at its edge.

items_markdown: Epithelia are sheets of tightly packed cells on a basement membrane, with little matrix and no blood vessels; they arise from all three germ layers.
Connective tissues have few cells in a large secreted matrix; the matrix is fluid in blood, flexible in cartilage and mineralised in bone.
Bone has osteocytes in lacunae joined by canaliculi and a rich blood supply; cartilage has chondrocytes, no canaliculi and no blood vessels.
Skeletal muscle is striated, multinucleate and voluntary; smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary; cardiac muscle is striated, branched, involuntary and myogenic.
Tendons join muscle to bone, ligaments join bone to bone; nervous tissue is made of neurones and supporting neuroglia.
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size; convert all lengths to the same unit before you divide.
